title: Yong Zhen Zhou: Who Controls the Controller? Thinking about physical player interactions
speaker: Yong Zhen Zhou
talk_title: Who Controls the Controller? Thinking about physical player interactions
description: Ever considered how the way you press a button can change your gaming experience? In this talk, I'll share my perspective as someone from an industrial design background overthinking the weird world of alternative controller (or alt.ctrl) games. Here the controller is as much a part of the game as what is in the screen. We’ll explore how controls like making funny faces, rocking on a chair, or shoveling golf balls, can extend the boundaries of a game experience and how the interaction changes the relationship between player and game. We'll also consider how these principles could apply to traditional games, challenging control conventions to offer a more varied and engaging experience

ZHEN ZOU: Hello, everyone. Nice to meet y'all. It is an honor to be here. It is my first time giving
a talk like this so it is going to be pretty interesting. Yeah. So first slide is basically
just about myself. My day job is a human computer interaction researchers so like HCI and I work in
an out fit national University of Singapore. I have made two alternative control games and
maybe that establishes me as such a designer. One is called pastry panic with where you have sliders

thinking about physical controller interactions through the lens of our controls. That's kind of
where I enter this space. I have been kind of showing this work for a while. What is
alt.ctrl? It stands for alternative control. It basically means any game that is -- I don't
think there is a fixed definition but it means any that is played with a non-conventional controller.
No keyboard and mouse and no game pad here. The people who make alt.ctrl are like this kind of
person where there is a perfectly good controller there but they would rather use a plunger. Some
examples of what I would consider alt.ctrl games. We have old arcade games. The one on the left you
roll a ball and you are an armadillo so you are rolling the armadillo. In the middle is police
911-2 I believe. And on the right is I believe thunder plate, a helicopter simulator where you
sit on the chair, and you look downwards. By moving the lever, the whole chair moves
so there is a motion effect even though there is no mechanical motion rig there. Following this,
I have some controls that I have seen over the years. This one is the book ritual where
you kind of talk with this living paper shredder and there are lots of books around and you write
stuff. You take the pages and eventually shred them. It is an interesting kind of
therapy experience which involves shredding what we normally consider precious items. This one is
Line Wobbler which is a one dimensional Dungeon Crawler played on a single LED strip with a door
stopper I believe. A spring door stopper as the input controller because it wobbles very nicely.
And this is Space box where quite literally you are in a spaceship but your controller is a box.
How not to get hit by a self-driving car which is a self-driving car plus an identification
algorithm. You try to get to the end of the road without it figuring out you are a person. This
one is coal rush. It is train simulator and rather than shoveling coal you shovel golf
balls and there is a hole in the middle of the train where you toot the horn and you break your
back basically shoving fake coal. Ruins climber you climb the ruins as a chicken and do so by
pulling a towel/rope. I have a GIF for this one. It isn't playing. Never mind. No GIFs. You kind of
just reeling that downwards and the chicken goes upwards. This one is planet licker. There is a
controller you must lick to lick the planet. There is a website called shakethatbutton got com which
is a user catalog of alt.ctrl games with a lot of history and links. If any of this interests you,
you can take a peek at that. Just a lid little introduction to the wide scope alt.ctrl can
encompass from the different ways of imputing and using cameras and something physical like
the shoveling. What I find fascinating is by how redesigning the controller of the
game it expends what constitutes the game. The conventional game experience is more or less
about designing the digital aspect. What happens behind the screen. When you do alt.ctrl design,
you are designing the interface, the controller but sometimes both the display which controls
input and output from the game, and should that expand into the real world. Suddenly
the game experience that may have been confined to the space between the hands
involves the people around you, the space around you, the condition of your body, how you move. It
literally expands the fantasy of the game world to something in our physical space rather than just
being on the screen in front of us. Imagine you are playing a little horror game. Please pardon
the art. It involves the lights turning on and off. You have a nice system in the house that lets
you control the house. As you play the game, the lights may turn off in the house one by one and
you need to turn them back on. If not it is like a health bar. While you are away from the screen at
the same time maybe there is a monster chasing you. But by using your lights,
the world of the game has expanded to encompass the entire household and things like the distance
between the screen and lights, how fast you can run, is there anyone else in the house that can
help you turn on the lights, and all these become part of the game experience. Thus when
alt.ctrl games are developed, considerations like what contest the game is being played in,
how much space it will take, how does it feel for the person to use or hold the controller,
is it physically possible to do an action, would anyone want to do the action become factors when
deciding the game. You need to consider the person and how they are playing the game. But
like mechanics in the digital part of games, these available aspects which become part of the game,
can be used to design the game experience. For example, you could try to pull in some real world
aspects as balance. Perhaps there is a tangible cost to a certain action which limits it. Rather
than having something like a consumable inventory, stamina bar, you have a tangible book that you rip
and now you have no book because it is gone. Or rather than having stamina you can have your own
physical stamina limiting the game. Or perhaps you could have a sanity cost by having people do
things they normally wouldn't do like licking a controller or shouting in a public space or
doing a silly dance. You force people to do these things instead of giving them a cool action. There
is always a semantic aspect to the controller and this immersive aspect. All these things are going
in. Like how does the way you control an object relate to -- how does the way you control object
change how you relate to it on the screen? Let's say you are playing Mario and normally you press
A to jump. You are like a puppeteer for Mario. If it was suddenly voice controlled your role is
like a drill sergeant. That changes the semantics of the experience and the whole thing kind of. So
alt.ctrl design involves recognizing the physical experience of the players interfacing with the
controller. How can this relate back to regular games with regular controllers? This is maybe
just overthinking things but I think there are already many games that take advantage of this.
One genre is fighting games which is maybe a bit unsurprising because fighting games have their
roots in the arcade. But specifically in fighting games what I would like to talk about are motion
inputs. The going back and forth and things that make it difficult to do certain special moves in
the game. There is a very nice YouTube channel called core A-gaming which has an amazing video
about this topic. Please check it out if you are interested. But just to go to it briefly,
a motion input kind of puts a physical cost for a stronger attack. There is this relation because
your character is exerting themselves to do a special attack. Therefore the player should also
exert themselves more as a similar cost. That's meant to be a GIF but no GIFs. And then also,
a motion input can put a physical limit on how and when you can use a move. Gal in sonic boom
needs to hold down and backwards to charge it. Therefore you cannot use this attack while you
are moving forward and it is a physical thing you just have to deal with. There is another mechanic
in fighting games and this is called burst. It is more or less a breaker mechanic that you can do
when your opponent is kind of hitting you a lot and you want them to just go away and give you
breathing room. The input for this controller, for this action, is to press all four attack buttons
on the controller. So if you see it, there is about seven button holes there but I believe
five are being used. Pressing four buttons is like slamming the table. If you played that on a game
pad, it would be pressing all four buttons at the same time. It mimics what the character is doing
because they are exerting themselves and pressing all four gives the feeling of get off of me. But
to give an example that is a bit closer to home here since we are all roguelike players, sorry. My
slides are wrong. Talk about game pad triggers. They have evolved to be more weapon-like.
And because of this the trigger is actually harder and takes more effort to press than just the old
button. While not only being used for FPS and shooting games to give the feeling of a weapon,
action games, take the trigger and its longer input as the input for heavy attacks or the
skills. Things that would seem to require more effort, again, require more effort on the player's
part. And for things like multi-button input, you press two buttons and get a powerful attack,
and more buttons means more power and effort for the player. Here is an example I think many of us
are familiar with. Slay the Spire and nice shifts. This is indeed a very nice feeling to be in when
your hand is just all shifts and you can play it with reckless abandon. But Slay the Spire is on
a few platforms now. There is mobile, console, and there is PC. While the game is the same,
I believe this feels superior on a mobile phone because when you play your shifts in this state,
you have to fling out the cards. I think that feels pretty good. Even while the
controller is not something that's designed by the creator's of the game,
in the end, every input the player makes on the controller still has a physical sensation
that contributes to the game's experience be it shoveling golf balls or pressing multiple
buttons at the same time. Considering the person behind controlling the controller and being aware
of them could lead to perhaps some interesting experiences when designing games. Especially
